(2) Boron surface segregation smears interfaces and leaves 1e17-1e18 B in channels, shifting Vt and raising leakage. (3) Porosification needs a current path to every buried p+ layer.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Raise contrast with 3e20 B plus C, or use bias-selective electrochemical etch stops (n/p+ pairs). (2) Carbon co-doping, lower growth temperature, thin intrinsic spacers, and counter-doping of channels. (3) Anodize from the slit with the substrate as back contact; intrinsic Si conducts enough at mA/cm2 anodization densities [ESTIMATE].
ideas.million_dollar_demo: ~$250k: buy or grow 10-40-pair Si/Si:B superlattices (university RPCVD or epi service), etch slits, measure per-layer HNA and anodization recess rates, SIMS boron profiles, XRD/TEM dislocations vs 20-120 pairs; then build floating-body or 1T1C test transistors on the freed layers.
ideas.resource_angle: Cuts the 3D-DRAM germanium exposure A2 identified (6-38% of world refined Ge at fleet scale) by 5-16x or to zero, removing a Chinese-controlled input.
ideas.us_buildable: University RPCVD epitaxy (Princeton, UT Austin, MIT.nano) or an epi service; characterization at NIST CNST and Brookhaven CFN.
ideas.triage_reason: Boron contracts Si by ~5.2e-24 cm3 per atom: 0.05% strain at 1e20 and 0.16% at 3e20 cm-3, matching the card; HNA and electrochemical porosification preferentially attack p+ Si. Selectivity over 0.3-1 um recesses and boron out-diffusion are measurable risks.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: p+/i selectivity <100:1 over a 0.5 um lateral recess, or channel boron >1e17 cm-3 after the full thermal budget.
ideas.claim_short: Si / Si:B dopant-contrast superlattice replaces Si/SiGe for 3D Si DRAM: misfit 0.84% -> 0.05-0.16%, Ge-free

ideas.name: Etch-compensated graded tier stack: uniform lateral recess by composition grading
ideas.one_liner: Pre-cancel the depth-dependent lateral recess that limits 3D DRAM by grading each tier's sacrificial-film composition so its etch rate rises exactly where etchant supply falls: zero added masks, ~2x taller decks.
ideas.mechanism: 3D DRAM sets each cell's channel and capacitor length by a lateral recess from a vertical hole or slit, and Lam notes that recess sizes vary along the stack because the etchant depletes with depth. Instead of fighting that with chemistry, pre-compensate at deposition: ramp each tier's sacrificial composition with depth (Ge fraction in SiGe, Si/N ratio and hydrogen content in SiN, or boron level in B3-06 layers) so the intrinsic etch rate rises where etchant supply falls. Calibrate the profile once per stack recipe from per-tier TEM; the only tool knob is a gas-flow ramp. Finish with a few tens of lateral atomic-layer-etch cycles to trim the last nanometres uniformly.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #2 (lateral recess uniformity named by Lam; tier economics) and A1 #1 (Cs spread sets the worst-case cell, because Cs scales with horizontal capacitor length).
ideas.step_change_claim: Recess spread +-12.5% -> +-2.5%: 8% smaller cell pitch along the recess and 11% higher worst-case Cs at 64 tiers; or ~2x taller deck (~130 vs ~66 tiers) per hole etch at equal uniformity, halving decks and HAR etches.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Diffusion-reaction (Thiele) model: rate(bottom)/rate(top) = 1/cosh(H/lambda). Calibrating a 25% drop at H = 4 um gives lambda = 5.0 um; then 8 um (133 tiers) -> 0.39x (grading range 2.6x) and 12 um -> 0.18x (5.5x). With a 600 nm recess plus 60 nm spacing, pitch 735 nm at +-12.5% vs 675 nm at +-2.5% (-8.2%); worst-case Cs 0.875 -> 0.975 of nominal. ALE trim of 20 nm at 0.5 nm/cycle = 40 cycles (600 nm by ALE alone would take 1,200 cycles). (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-07)

ideas.resource_angle: No new materials or masks; fewer decks and HAR etches cut fluorocarbon gas use and etch-tool time.

ideas.triage_reason: Transport-limited recess is deterministic and periodic, so grading etch rate with depth is process-control physics.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: run-to-run transport variation exceeds the compensable systematic part.

ideas.name: Vt-coded in-stack tier decoder: kill the staircase so 3D DRAM lines can be short
ideas.one_liner: Replace the 3D-NAND staircase (~0.5 um per tier) with a binary decoder built into the stack: each tier's line passes 2*log2(N) select gates whose depletion/enhancement pattern encodes the tier number, shrinking line-end area 12-21x.
ideas.mechanism: 3D NAND reaches each tier's horizontal line through a staircase whose length grows with tier count; DRAM wants short lines (sub-page activation, low RC), and at 64 tiers a ~32 um staircase is longer than a 512-cell line. Instead, route every tier's horizontal line under 2*log2(N) vertical select-gate pillars before it merges into one common vertical contact. In each tier, each select region is permanently depletion-mode (always on) or enhancement-mode according to that tier's binary address, so driving the pillars with an address and its complement opens exactly one tier's path. The code is written per tier during deposition with one coarse (um-scale, i-line) block mask, or, as in Macronix-style LSM for 3D NAND, by programming charge-trap select gates once at test.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #2 (3D tier area and economics) and A1 #8 (page overfetch: short wordlines enable sub-page activation).
ideas.step_change_claim: Line-termination area 12x smaller at 64 tiers (32 um staircase -> 2.7 um) and 21x at 128; line-end overhead for a 128-cell line 83% -> 30%, enabling 4x shorter wordlines and correspondingly less activation overfetch.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Staircase = N x 0.5 um [ASSUMPTION]; decoder = 2*ceil(log2 N) x 0.2 um + 0.3 um contact: N = 64 -> 2.7 um, N = 128 -> 3.1 um. Overhead for a 128-cell (6.4 um) line: 32/(32+6.4) = 83% -> 2.7/(2.7+6.4) = 30%; for 512 cells 56% -> 10%. Select-string RC: 12 x ~2 kOhm (wide oxide TFTs at the block edge) x 50 fF = 1.2 ns. Coding cost by mask: 64 coarse exposures at ~$5-10 [ASSUMPTION] = $320-640/wafer; by one-time programming: zero masks. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-08)

ideas.resource_angle: Fewer staircase trim/etch cycles and less area per bit; no new materials.

ideas.triage_reason: Depletion/enhancement select gates are ordinary transistors, and series resistance on (capacitive) wordlines is tolerable.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: oxide select-gate Vt split cannot keep >0.5 V margin after 10-year-equivalent PBTI at 85 C.
ideas.claim_short: Vt-coded binary tier decoder replaces the staircase: line-end area 12-21x smaller

ideas.name: Sandwich stack: Smart-Cut single-crystal sense layers every 16 oxide tiers
ideas.one_liner: Interleave a transferred single-crystal Si layer with 400 C CMOS sense amps every 16 oxide-channel tiers, so every vertical bitline is 16 cells tall and the in-tier capacitor shrinks from ~600 nm to ~30-60 nm.
ideas.mechanism: Build oxide-channel 3D DRAM tiers (horizontal or vertical-channel 1T1C or 2T0C) in groups of 16, then bond a ~50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top by Smart Cut (H-implanted donor, low-temperature bond, split) and build n- and p-channel transistors in it at <=400 C, as CEA-Leti showed with full 2.5 V n&p SOI MOSFETs at 400 C (IEDM 2025, nanosecond laser anneal plus solid-phase regrowth). That layer holds the local sense amps, tier decoders and muxes for the 16 tiers below; the next 16 tiers go on top. Each vertical bitline is only 16 cells tall (~2-4 fF), so a 1T1C cell needs only ~0.3-0.6 fF, which fits in a ~30-60 nm lateral capacitor inside the tier, shrinking the per-tier footprint from A1's ~0.03 um2 base case to ~0.01 um2. Global bitlines run up to a bonded or top-level periphery.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 and #2 together (the horizontal capacitor sets the 3D footprint), A1 #10 (short bitlines allow low VARY), and the weak p-type oxide that limits in-tier sensing (B2-08).
ideas.step_change_claim: In-tier capacitor 600 nm -> 31-59 nm; per-tier footprint ~3x smaller; 64 tiers -> ~4.5 Gb/mm2 (10x 1-beta) and ~5-7x bits/$ before yield.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Vertical BL: 16 x 0.08 fF + 1 um x 0.2 fF/um + 0.5 fF SA = 1.98 fF (30:1 mux -> 3.78 fF). A1 criterion -> Cs 0.31 (0.59) fF. In-tier MIM with ~160 nm perimeter at EOT 0.55 nm = 0.010 fF/nm -> 31 (59) nm long. Footprint 50 x 200 nm -> 0.070 Gb/mm2 per tier (eff 0.70); 64 tiers 4.48 Gb/mm2. Cost $2,000 base + 64 x $30-45 + 4 sense layers x $400-700 = $5,520-7,680 -> 5.0-6.9x bits/$ before yield. Sense area: one ~0.3 um2 latch per 30 vertical bitlines -> 30:1 mux. Smart-Cut H dose ~5e16 cm-2 vs a 1.4e11 cm-2 donor budget: the barrier must block 99.9997%. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-09)

(2) 400 C-stable channels (In-poor IGZO, IGO, ALD In2O3 shown to survive 600 C at Purdue). (3) Larger groups (32 tiers per sense layer, 60:1 mux).

ideas.resource_angle: No Ge superlattice, no EUV (F 40-50 nm); Smart-Cut donors are reclaimable bulk wafers.

ideas.name: H-free sputtered-Si laser grains as in-stack CMOS and floating-body tiers
ideas.one_liner: Excimer-laser-crystallize sputtered (hydrogen-free) amorphous Si into location-controlled single-crystal grains between oxide tiers, giving in-stack p- and n-FETs 8-17x stronger than p-oxide and floating-body cells without epitaxy, Ge or a hydrogen implant.
ideas.mechanism: Sputter amorphous Si at ~100 C (no PECVD hydrogen) over ~0.5-1 um of SiO2 that carries a lattice of small grain-filter holes, then melt it with an excimer-laser pulse: the mu-Czochralski process grows one location-controlled single-crystal grain (3-7.5 um) from each hole, with electron/hole mobilities of 460-510 / 121-250 cm2/Vs reported by the Delft group. The ~100 ns pulse heats only the top ~0.3 um, so oxide tiers below stay cool. Use the grains for (a) complementary sense amps and decoders inside the stack, without Smart Cut's hydrogen implant (B3-09's main risk), and (b) floating-body capacitor-less 1T cells, which need holes and therefore cannot be made in n-type IGZO, for Ge-free 3D silicon DRAM tiers.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #2 (a 3D silicon cell without epitaxial Si/SiGe), A3 section 2.4 (floating body needs a p-capable channel), and the hydrogen show-stopper of B3-09.
ideas.step_change_claim: In-stack p-FET drive 8-17x that of a p-type oxide TFT with zero implanted hydrogen; Ge-free, epi-free floating-body tiers (1-beta parity at ~17 tiers, 1 bit).
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Mobility: single-grain p 121-250 vs p-oxide ~15 cm2/Vs -> 8-17x drive. Floating-body 10F2 at F = 40 nm, 60% of area inside usable grains, eff 0.70 -> 0.026 Gb/mm2 per tier; parity at 17 tiers. Thermal diffusion length in SiO2 for a 100 ns pulse = sqrt(8.6e-7 m2/s x 1e-7 s) = 0.29 um -> 0.5-1 um isolation per laser tier, so laser tiers stack at ~1 um pitch; use them as every-16th-tier sense layers rather than as every tier. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-10)

ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Twins and defects inside grains raise leakage and variability (fatal for floating-body retention). (2) Grain pitch (~3-7 um) wastes ~40% of area and forces mats to tile to the grain lattice. (3) Laser coupling, debris and the ~1 um isolation layers make deep vias.

ideas.resource_angle: No Ge, no epitaxy, no hydrogen implant; excimer lasers are mature display tools (but neon laser gas is an A2 chokepoint).
ideas.us_buildable: Columbia University (laser crystallization heritage) [UNVERIFIED-PK] or Penn State; devices at Penn Singh Center or Cornell CNF.
ideas.triage_reason: Location-controlled single-grain Si TFTs are demonstrated (Delft mu-Czochralski); used for sense CMOS they tolerate intra-grain defects. Floating-body storage in grains is riskier (twins raise leakage) but optional.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: grain-located FETs show Vt sigma >50 mV, making SAs unworkable at 16-tier pitch.

ideas.name: Memory interposer: oxide gain-cell tiers built into the silicon interposer
ideas.one_liner: AI packages sit on 2,700-4,700 mm2 of silicon interposer that carries only wires; build 8 tiers of BEOL oxide gain cells into it and every package gains ~21-250 GB at ~0.3 pJ/bit with no added footprint.
ideas.mechanism: Large AI packages use a silicon interposer that carries only wires and TSVs. Build 8 tiers of BEOL oxide gain cells (B3-04 coax cells, or A3-style vertical 2T0C) into the interposer's metal stack at <=400 C on the 65 nm-class line that makes interposers, with stitched periodic arrays under the GPU and HBM footprints and keep-outs around TSVs and bump fields. The GPU reads this memory straight down through its existing micro-bumps or hybrid bonds, adding a capacity tier between on-die SRAM and HBM with no extra footprint. Oxide cells hold >200 s at 95 C (imec), so the hot interposer is acceptable.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 data-movement energy, A1 #6 HBM tax, A2 white space 1 (capacity per cleanroom-hour using silicon already being bought).
ideas.step_change_claim: +21-145 GB per package on a 2,700 mm2 interposer (up to ~250 GB on 4,700 mm2) at ~0.3 pJ/bit vs 3.5 for HBM, for ~$100-240 of added tier cost per interposer.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Usable 65%: 2,700 mm2 -> 1,755 mm2. 10F2 vertical 2T0C at F = 65 nm, 1 bit x 8 tiers, eff 0.508 -> 21 GB; coax 4F2, 2 bits x 8, eff 0.70 -> 145 GB (4,719 mm2: 37-254 GB). Cost: 8 tiers x $200-475 / 16 interposers per wafer = $100-238 per interposer. Energy: bump hop 0.05-0.1 + activation 0.18 + on-die 0.05 = ~0.3 pJ/bit. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-11)

ideas.name: Photonic periphery wafer: every bonded DRAM die is born with optical I/O
ideas.one_liner: Next-generation DRAM already makes its periphery on a separate bonded wafer; make that wafer in a monolithic silicon-photonics CMOS process so each memory die talks over fiber at ~3.4 pJ/bit, with capacity no longer limited by HBM beachfront or TSV stacks.
ideas.mechanism: Samsung's 4F2 DRAM builds the periphery on a separate wafer bonded under the cells. Make that periphery wafer in a monolithic photonics-CMOS process (microring modulators, Ge photodetectors, waveguides and 45 nm-class transistors on one wafer) so every DRAM die has optical I/O built in. The memory die connects to compute over fibers or a photonic interposer at metre scale, so capacity is not limited by the 8-12 HBM stacks that fit around a GPU or by TSV stacks. Closed-loop heaters keep the rings locked as DRAM die temperature moves.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV tax and beachfront, A1 #5 (off-package DDR at ~10-20 pJ/bit), A2 (HBM takes ~3x wafer per GB).
ideas.step_change_claim: DRAM at a distance at ~3.4 pJ/bit (HBM parity) instead of ~10-20 pJ/bit for off-package DDR [UNVERIFIED], ~500 GB/s per die, and unlimited capacity per accelerator; no TSVs or HBM stacking on the memory side. Energy is NOT better than HBM today.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Link: 2.4 pJ/bit electronics + 0.7 pJ/bit laser (Celestial AI, Hot Chips 2025, company claim) + 0.3 array = 3.4 pJ/bit vs HBM 3.5. Bandwidth: 8 fibers x 16 wavelengths x 32 Gb/s = 4 Tb/s = 500 GB/s per die. Ring tuning: 256 rings x 2-5 mW = 0.5-1.3 W = 0.13-0.32 pJ/bit. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-12)

absorbed_cards.name: Photonic periphery wafer bonded under the DRAM cell array
absorbed_cards.one_liner: Incumbents already bond the DRAM cell wafer onto a separate periphery wafer. Make that wafer a CMOS-photonics wafer, so every die speaks light at ~2-3 pJ/bit without an interposer.
absorbed_cards.mechanism: 4F^2 VCT and 3D DRAM programmes (Samsung 10a VCT, VS-DRAM, SK hynix VG) all wafer-bond the periphery to the cell array. Here that periphery wafer is a monolithic CMOS + silicon-photonics process: 45 nm-class SOI with microring modulators, Ge photodiodes and WDM filters. It carries the global periphery (command decode, SerDes, ECC and codecs from B4-01/07) plus 8-16-wavelength microring transceivers. Sense amps and local drivers stay on the cell wafer, bonded to the photonic wafer at 1-10 um pitch. Each die exits through 2-4 waveguides edge-coupled to fibre or a photonic interposer, with an external laser source. Memory can then sit 1-10 m away on cool sleds (B4-13) or in pools. For capacity tiers, HBM's silicon interposer and TSV I/O tax disappear.
absorbed_cards.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 interface energy, #6 HBM tax, #7 periphery; enables B4-13
absorbed_cards.step_change_claim: ~2-3 pJ/bit at metre reach (vs HBM 3.4-3.5 pJ/bit at millimetre reach and DDR5 ~10-20 pJ/bit), using DDR-density dies at ~1x DDR5 wafer per bit instead of HBM's 3x.
absorbed_cards.first_principles_estimate: 16 wavelengths x 32 Gb/s (or 8 x 64) = 64 GB/s per waveguide, so a 128 GB/s die needs 2 waveguides. Energy: modulator + driver + receiver ~1 pJ/b, laser wall-plug ~1 pJ/b, ring thermal tuning 0.1-1 pJ/b, total 2-3 pJ/b [ESTIMATE]. For calibration, Celestial reports ~6.2 pJ/b (2024) and ~2.4 pJ/b (2025) per memory transaction, vs ~62.5 via NVLink/NVSwitch. (card14)

ideas.triage_reason: Merged with B4-14. Monolithic Si photonics and bonded periphery both exist. Physics constraints: microring resonances drift ~0.1 nm/K next to a heat-sensitive array, and 45 nm-class photonic transistors are too large for under-array sense amps, so only global periphery/SerDes can go photonic. Energy reaches HBM parity, not better; the gain is capacity at distance.

ideas.name: Coil-stacked HBM: inductive links instead of TSVs, NAND-style wire-bonded power
ideas.one_liner: Stack thinned DRAM dies that talk through ~2,000 small coils placed over their arrays and take power through edge wire bonds, removing TSV keep-out and TSV/bump yield loss from HBM (energy per bit is not improved).
ideas.mechanism: Replace HBM's through-silicon vias and micro-bumps with inductive-coupling links: each thinned DRAM die carries ~2,000 small coils in its top metal over the array, and data hop vertically between dies by magnetic coupling (Keio's ThruChip Interface). Power enters the way NAND stacks do it: staggered dies with wire bonds, or a few coarse power vias at the die edge. The DRAM die loses its TSV keep-out field and the stack loses TSV/bump yield loss; coils also tolerate several um of misalignment, so stacking needs no fine-pitch alignment.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV/stacking tax (~3x wafer per bit; die +35-45%, yield -20-30%), and hybrid bonding's slip to HBM4E/HBM5.
ideas.step_change_claim: HBM wafer-per-bit tax 3x -> ~2.0-2.3x (+28-50% HBM bits per wafer) with no hybrid-bonding dependence. Energy is NOT improved: ~0.7 pJ/bit per coil hop vs ~0.15 pJ/bit per TSV layer.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Coils: 2,048 x (50 um)^2 = 5.1 mm2 placed over the array. If TSV keep-out plus TSV/bump yield loss make up 33-50% of the HBM tax, the tax falls from 3.0x to 2.34-2.0x, i.e., +28-50% bits per wafer. Energy: Shiba (Hot Chips 2022, 7 nm SRAM) 0.7 pJ/bit at 8.5 Gb/s per link vs A1's ~0.15 pJ/bit per TSV layer, so worse. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-13)

ideas.novelty: KNOWN (Kuroda/Keio, ThruChip) + TWIST: applied to 12-16-high HBM-class stacks with NAND-style wire-bonded power and coils over the DRAM array.

absorbed_cards.name: TSV-free inductive stacking for short memory-on-logic stacks
absorbed_cards.one_liner: Replace TSVs and microbumps with on-chip coils (ThruChip-style inductive coupling) in 2-4-high DRAM-on-logic stacks. That removes the TSV process and part of the HBM area tax, but the physics limits it to short stacks.
absorbed_cards.mechanism: Dies thinned to ~10 um are glued rather than bump-bonded. Data crosses between stacked dies through pairs of ~30 um on-chip spiral coils at ~8 Gb/s each. Power and ground use a few highly doped silicon vias or edge connections. There is no TSV etch or fill, no microbump yield loss and no hybrid-bond overlay.
absorbed_cards.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV/stacking tax (~3x wafer per bit); A1 #5 data movement (memory directly on logic).
absorbed_cards.step_change_claim: For 4-high stacks: no TSV or microbump process steps, ~26% less die area than TSVs (reported for a 7 nm SRAM stack), and ~2.7 pJ/b on the worst-case hop. For 16-high HBM it fails: 62-562 mm2 of coil per die, or 13.5 pJ/b through relays.
absorbed_cards.first_principles_estimate: HBM4-class bandwidth of 2,048 x 8 Gb/s = 16.4 Tb/s needs 1,928 links at 8.5 Gb/s. Coil diameter must roughly match the coupling distance. A 16-high stack of 30 um dies needs 450 um coils, i.e. 562 mm2 of coil per die (impossible); with 10 um dies, 62 mm2 (still impossible); a 4-high stack of 10 um dies needs 2 mm2 (fine). The relay alternative costs 0.9 pJ/b per hop, 13.5 pJ/b to the top of a 16-high stack against ~3-4 pJ/b for HBM in total. (research/models/B5_firstprinciples_estimates.py section B5-18)

absorbed_cards.show_stoppers: (1) Coupling reach scales with coil diameter, so tall stacks need huge coils. (2) Power delivery still needs vias. (3) Bandwidth density (2.7 Gb/s/mm2 for 2015-era relays) is far below hybrid bonding.
absorbed_cards.revival_or_workaround: (1) Restrict to 4-high or less, and get height from monolithic tiers instead (B3/B4). (2) Highly doped silicon vias for power. (3) Raise per-link rates with resonant coupling.
absorbed_cards.million_dollar_demo: An MPW logic die plus a DRAM-like test die with coils, thinned to 10-20 um and glue-stacked 2-4 high at a packaging lab; measure BER, pJ/b and crosstalk (~$300k).
absorbed_cards.resource_angle: Removes TSV copper fill and microbump solder (Sn, Ag) and lowers stacking capital; adds no scarce elements.

ideas.triage_reason: Merged with B5-18. Inductive links are demonstrated (Keio/ThruChip). B5-18's reach arithmetic holds: coupling distance scales with coil diameter, so direct top-to-base links in a 16-high stack need 62-562 mm2 of coils per die. Per-die relays work but cost ~0.7 pJ/b per hop: 6.0 pJ/b average and 11.2 pJ/b worst at 16-high (C0-12) vs ~3.5 pJ/b for HBM. Valid as a wafer-per-bit play; energy-negative above ~8-high.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive (<=4-high direct; taller only as a capacity tier). Kill test: >2,000 coils over the arrays couple >5 mV into sense amps, or edge-bonded power cannot deliver ~60 W.
ideas.claim_short: TSV-free inductive-coupling stacks: no TSV keep-out/yield loss; direct for 2-4-high, relayed above
dead_subclaims: Direct (non-relayed) inductive links through 12-16-high stacks: 62-562 mm2 of coil per die

ideas.name: Sidewall-wired DRAM cube with adaptive (die-position-corrected) side-face lithography
ideas.one_liner: Stack thinned DRAM dies with no TSVs, polish the cube face, and write the vertical bus on it with maskless laser lithography that adapts to each die's real position: 1,250-2,500 wires per face and plated side power rails.
ideas.mechanism: Thin DRAM dies to 30-50 um, stack them with 2-5 um adhesive and no TSVs, then polish one or two faces of the cube to expose edge pads that each die routes to its edge. Pattern the vertical bus on the face with maskless laser direct imaging that first measures each die's actual position and adapts the wiring (adaptive patterning, as in fan-out packaging), so several um of die misplacement do not matter. Plated Cu stripes ~10 um thick carry power along the same face, and a base logic die at the bottom connects to the side bus.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 TSV tax and hybrid-bonding slip; HBM height limits (775-1,000 um).
ideas.step_change_claim: TSV-free HBM-class stack: removes TSV keep-out and TSV/bond yield loss (HBM tax 3x -> ~2x [ESTIMATE]); 2,500-5,000 bus wires on two faces; 20-high stacks in under 1 mm.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Edge 10 mm at 4-8 um pitch = 1,250-2,500 wires per face. Vertical side wire 16 x 50 um = 0.8 mm, 160 fF -> 0.026 pJ/bit at 0.4 V swing. Penalty: each die routes ~5 mm to its edge: +1.0 pJ/bit at 0.2 pJ/bit/mm full swing, +0.25 pJ/bit at 0.05 pJ/bit/mm low swing. Power rail 10 um x 200 um x 0.8 mm = 6.8 mOhm. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-14)

ideas.name: Origami memory stack: one thin membrane folded into N layers, wired through the folds [SPECULATIVE]
ideas.one_liner: Build N memory dies as one continuous BEOL-only membrane on a glass carrier, release it and fold it accordion-style into an HBM-like stack whose vertical wiring is simply the metal running around each fold: no TSVs, no bumps, no die alignment.
ideas.mechanism: Build N memory die images side by side as one continuous thin membrane (an oxide-cell array plus 3-4 metal levels, ~1.5-3 um thick) on a glass carrier with a laser-release layer, wiring neighbouring dies together across the gaps with ordinary BEOL lines. Release the membrane and fold it accordion-style into an N-layer stack bonded with thin adhesive, with fold radii of ~150-300 um. Vertical connectivity is the BEOL wiring that runs continuously around each fold, so there are no TSVs, no micro-bumps and no die-to-die alignment. The folded stack lands on a logic base die like HBM.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV/stacking tax, A2 (HBM wafer intensity).
ideas.step_change_claim: [SPECULATIVE] HBM-like stacks at near-planar wafer cost per bit: stacking tax 3x -> ~1.05-1.1x (fold loss 4.5-8.6%), with 20,000+ vertical wires per fold.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Fold radius R = t/(2*eps): t = 3 um, eps = 0.5% -> 300 um; fold length pi*R = 0.94 mm; loss 8.6% per 10 mm layer. t = 1.5 um -> 150 um, 0.47 mm, 4.5%. Wires across a 10 mm fold at 1 um pitch x 2 metals = 20,000. Thermal: 16 adhesive layers of 2 um at 0.2 W/mK = 1.6 K cm2/W, similar to conventional micro-bump stacks (1.54) and worse than bumpless WOW (0.46). (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-15)

ideas.novelty: [SPECULATIVE] NEW combination: foldable thin-film electronics and BEOL-only memory exist separately; folding one membrane into a memory stack with wiring through the folds was not found.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Cracking of BEOL dielectrics and metal at the folds (0.5% strain assumed) and fold reliability over thermal cycling. (2) Handling and folding um-thin membranes at production throughput. (3) Defect yield of an N-times-larger continuous membrane.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Fold zones with polymer-only dielectric and serpentine Cu (stretchable-electronics practice), or larger fold radius. (2) Fold on-carrier using hinge-release lines and plate tooling. (3) Fuse or laser-cut a bad layer out of the bus and carry spare layers (B3-19 arithmetic).
ideas.million_dollar_demo: ~$150k: fold a 4-layer membrane of daisy-chain wiring plus a small oxide TFT array built on polyimide-on-glass at a university fab; cycle-test the folds and measure continuity and TFT drift.
ideas.resource_angle: No TSV or bonding tools; BEOL-only processing on reusable glass carriers.
ideas.us_buildable: Flexible-electronics facilities (ASU, Penn State) [UNVERIFIED-PK], Purdue Birck.
ideas.triage_reason: Thin-film mechanics allows it: a 5 um brittle membrane at 0.5% strain needs R=500 um (1 mm layer pitch, too tall), but a 2 um polymer hinge with neutral-plane Cu at 3% strain needs R~33 um (67 um layer pitch, HBM-like) (C0-13). Heat must cross 16 polymer interfaces (~8 K/W over 100 mm2: 24 K at 3 W, 120 K at 15 W), so it suits low-power oxide capacity memory, not hot DRAM.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: <=1 um-pitch Cu in 33 um-radius folds fails thermal cycling (-40/125 C, 1,000 cycles).
ideas.claim_short: Origami stack: one thin membrane folded N times, wired through the folds; stacking tax 3x -> 1.05-1.1x

ideas.name: Yield firewall: spare tiers per block plus pre-tested tier groups
ideas.one_liner: Treat 3D DRAM tiers like NAND blocks but finer: carry 4 spare tiers per block, fused in through a programmable tier decoder, and build very tall stacks from tested 8-tier groups, so 64 tiers need a 0.5% per-tier defect rate instead of 0.2%.
ideas.mechanism: Build 64 + s tiers per block and fuse out up to s defective tiers per block through the tier decoder (B3-08 makes tier selection programmable), so one killer defect in one tier no longer kills a block. For very tall stacks, build tiers in groups of 8 on separate carriers, run parametric tests on each group (vertical-bitline continuity, leakage, Vt maps from built-in test structures), and stack only good groups by die-to-wafer hybrid bonding. That turns a multiplicative 64-tier yield into a sum of 8-tier yields plus bond yields.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #2 compound tier yield (SK hynix's 5 tiers at 56.1% imply ~0.89 per tier; 64 tiers need >=0.998 per tier after repair).
ideas.step_change_claim: Required per-block-tier killer-defect rate relaxed 2.5x (0.2% -> 0.5%) for 6% area overhead at 97.5% die yield; pre-tested groups lift 64-tier stack yield from 53% to ~97% at 0.99 per tier.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Block survival P(<=s defects in 64+s tiers): p = 0.01: s=0 0.526, s=2 0.971, s=4 0.9994; p = 0.005: s=4 ~1.0000. Die of 1,000 blocks: p = 0.005, s = 4 -> 97.5% (6.25% overhead); p = 0.01, s = 4 -> 54%. Tested groups: 0.99^8 = 0.923 per group (bad groups discarded), 7 bonds at 99.5% -> 0.966 stack yield vs 0.99^64 = 0.526 monolithic. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-16)

ideas.name: Hydrogen-lean batch-furnace mold for oxide 3D DRAM
ideas.one_liner: Because the cell wafer is now separate from the periphery, deposit the whole 3D mold hot in a batch LPCVD furnace and out-gas it before any oxide channel goes in, shrinking the hydrogen reservoir next to each channel 4-8x.
ideas.mechanism: NAND-style oxide 3D DRAM needs a 32-128-pair SiO2/SiN mold; single-wafer PECVD films carry ~3-25 at.% hydrogen, and hydrogen drives IGZO Vt drift (H-doping under PBTI, which imec cut ~30x with an H+O anneal). With the periphery on a separate bonded wafer, the cell wafer's mold can be made hot: deposit the alternating stack in a batch LPCVD furnace (100-150 wafers per load, ~4% H in LPCVD SiN, <1% in high-temperature oxide), then out-gas it at 800-900 C before any oxide channel is deposited (for example by Kioxia-style SiN->IGZO replacement). Add per-tier ALD Al2O3 hydrogen barriers around the replacement channels and finish with an O-rich anneal instead of forming gas.
ideas.which_bottleneck: The multi-level drift doubt shared by every oxide 3D idea (A3 section 2.1 open problem 1; B2's biggest physics doubt) and A1 #3.
ideas.step_change_claim: Hydrogen reservoir next to each channel 4-8x smaller (PECVD SiN 4.8e16 -> LPCVD 1.1e16 H/cm2 per 30 nm tier, or 5.9e15 for oxide), relaxing the fraction allowed to reach the channel for a 20 mV (3-bit) budget from 3 ppm to 13-24 ppm; mold deposition at ~11 wafer-minutes per 64-pair stack.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: C_ox at EOT 3 nm = 1.15 uF/cm2 -> a 20 mV budget = 1.44e11 donors/cm2. 30 nm PECVD SiN (8e22 atoms/cm3, 20% H) = 4.8e16 H/cm2 -> only 3.0e-6 may reach the channel; LPCVD SiN (4% H) 1.1e16 -> 1.3e-5; PECVD TEOS oxide (3% H) 5.9e15 -> 2.4e-5. Batch: 64 x 30 nm SiN at 2.5 nm/min + 64 x 30 nm oxide at 8 nm/min + 128 x 5 min gas switching = 27.5 h per 150 wafers = 11 min per wafer. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-17)

ideas.resource_angle: Batch furnaces are cheap per wafer; fewer PECVD chambers; lower drift means less refresh.
ideas.us_buildable: Furnaces at Cornell CNF, Stanford SNF, Georgia Tech IEN; ERDA/SIMS at Sandia or PNNL EMSL.
ideas.triage_reason: Hydrogen content of LPCVD vs PECVD films and its role in IGZO Vt drift are established; the card's budget (20 mV = 1.4e11 donors/cm2 = 3 ppm of one PECVD SiN tier) makes this de-risking physics, not speculation.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: SIMS/ERDA shows ALD precursors or bonding dominate the channel H budget regardless of the mold.
ideas.claim_short: H-lean LPCVD batch mold, out-gassed before channel deposition: channel H reservoir 4-8x smaller

ideas.name: BEOL bonus tiers: oxide gain-cell tiers stacked on a finished Si DRAM die
ideas.one_liner: Seal a conventional 1-beta-class DRAM die with a hydrogen barrier and stack 8 tiers of oxide gain cells over the whole die, including the ~49% periphery that holds no bits today: 1.4-4.8x bits per die with no new front end.
ideas.mechanism: Take a conventional 1-beta-class DRAM die, give ~15% of its area to extra sense and write-verify circuits, and after its last metal and hydrogen alloy anneal, seal it with an Al2O3/SiN hydrogen barrier and deposit 8 tiers of oxide gain cells (coax 4F2 B3-04, or vertical 2T0C) over the whole die, periphery included. The fast Si 1T1C array remains the hot tier (~15 ns), and the oxide tiers above form a dense, low-refresh warm tier (~30-50 ns) in the same package and interface. The add-on is a BEOL module that a separate, cheaper fab could run on finished DRAM wafers.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A2 white space 1 (bits per cleanroom-hour and capex), A1 #7 (49% periphery area holds no bits), A1 #3.
ideas.step_change_claim: Bits per die 1.4-4.8x with no new front end: conservative (10F2, 1 bit x 8) 22.9 Gb on a 16 Gb die area; coax 1 bit 45.5 Gb (2.85x); coax 2 bit 77.5 Gb (4.8x); bits/$ 0.7-4.0x depending on $100-475 per tier.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Base 16 Gb x 0.85 = 13.6 Gb; added 36.5 mm2 x (0.254 / 0.875 / 1.75 Gb/mm2) = +9.3 / +31.9 / +63.9 Gb. Wafer $3,800 + 8 tiers x $100 (NAND-like single etch) to $475 (A3 convention): conservative 1.18x / 0.71x bits/$; coax 1b 2.35x / 1.42x; coax 2b 4.0x / 2.4x. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-18)

ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Hydrogen conflict: Si DRAM retention relies on hydrogen passivation while IGZO needs hydrogen kept out. (2) The base die must drive the new tiers, so it is a redesign, not a retrofit. (3) Two memory types in one die complicate test, repair and the controller.

ideas.million_dollar_demo: ~$300k: use DRAM test wafers or a university CMOS wafer as stand-in, cap with a hydrogen barrier, build 2-4 oxide tiers on top; measure Si interface-trap density and retention proxies before and after, plus oxide-cell retention.
ideas.resource_angle: Multiplies output of existing DRAM fabs without new cleanrooms (A2's binding constraint); the BEOL module could be onshore even if base wafers are not.
ideas.us_buildable: Micron Boise ID / Manassas VA (base wafers); BEOL module at SkyWater Bloomington MN or NY CREATES Albany; coupons at Purdue Birck.
ideas.triage_reason: Oxide-over-CMOS exists; the conflict is hydrogen (Si needs H passivation, IGZO needs H kept out), solvable by doing the H alloy anneal before an Al2O3/SiN cap.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: the Si DRAM retention tail degrades >2x after oxide-tier processing behind an H-blocking cap.
ideas.claim_short: Oxide gain-cell tiers stacked on a finished Si DRAM die (periphery included): 1.4-4.8x bits per die

ideas.name: Thin wafer-on-wafer DRAM with spare layers (64-high in today's package height)
ideas.one_liner: Stack DRAM wafers thinned to ~4-10 um with bumpless 1-2 um TSVs, carry 12.5% spare layers so wafer stacking survives bad die sites, and fit 64 layers into 640 um.
ideas.mechanism: Stack whole DRAM wafers thinned to ~4-10 um wafer-on-wafer with bumpless via-last TSVs of ~1-2 um diameter, the Tokyo Tech / WOW Alliance (BBCube) approach. Because wafer stacking cannot select known-good dies, add spare layers (18 for 16, or 72 for 64) and let the base die map out failed die sites layer by layer after in-die repair. Thin silicon makes each TSV ~20x smaller in area including keep-out and cuts stack thermal resistance ~3x versus bump stacks, and 10 um layers allow 64-high stacks inside today's package height.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV tax and the package height limit; hybrid bonding's slip.
ideas.step_change_claim: TSV+keep-out area ~21x smaller per TSV; 64-high stacks in 640 um (4x capacity per stack vs 16-high); stack yield 94-99% with 12.5% spare layers at >=95% die-site yield.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: TSV+keep-out (6 um + 2 x 5 um)^2 = 256 um2 vs (1.5 + 2 x 1)^2 = 12.2 um2. 64 x 10 um = 640 um. Yield: die-site y = 0.95 -> P(>=16 of 18) = 0.942, P(>=64 of 72) = 0.990 (16-high without spares: 0.44); y = 0.90 -> 0.73 / 0.71. Thermal: 0.46 vs 1.54 K cm2/W (WOW, 2017). (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-19)

ideas.name: Cold-bond stack: room-temperature surface-activated hybrid bonding for oxide memory
ideas.one_liner: Bond oxide-memory wafers at room temperature with Ar-beam surface activation instead of 350 C+ anneals, removing a post-bond thermal dose equal to ~5-37 years at 85 C of drift kinetics from every multi-layer stack.
ideas.mechanism: Standard hybrid bonding needs a post-bond anneal above ~350 C to close the Cu pads, and every sequential bond re-anneals everything below it. For oxide-channel memory wafers that cumulative heat (8-16 h at 350 C for an 8-layer stack) shifts Vt and redistributes hydrogen, which multi-level storage cannot tolerate. Use surface-activated bonding instead: Ar fast-atom-beam cleaning in ultra-high vacuum lets Cu-Cu (and, with Si nano-adhesion layers, dielectric) surfaces bond at room temperature without anneal. Memory layers can then be bonded after multi-level calibration and after hydrogen-sensitive steps, and heterogeneous layers (ferroelectric, photonic, organic) can join without a thermal limit.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A3 white space 3's named risk (the bonding thermal cycle shifts oxide Vt), the multi-level drift doubt, and A1 #6/#7 (bonding is now in every DRAM roadmap).
ideas.step_change_claim: Post-bond thermal budget 8-16 h at 350 C -> 0, removing a thermal dose equal to ~5-37 years at 85 C of activated drift kinetics per stack.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Acceleration exp(Ea/k x (1/358 K - 1/623 K)) for Ea = 0.58-0.72 eV (IGZO recovery/stress barriers, CPB 2015) = 2,960-20,400x; 16 h at 350 C ~ 5.4-37 years at 85 C. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-20)

ideas.name: Grow-the-hole: bottom-up dual area-selective deposition replaces the high-aspect-ratio etch [SPECULATIVE]
ideas.one_liner: Instead of etching um-deep holes through a 64-128-tier mold, grow the mold around metal pillars one tier at a time with selective tungsten on tungsten and selective dielectric on dielectric, then dissolve the pillars: perfectly vertical holes at AR 40-80 with no plasma etch.
ideas.mechanism: 3D memory molds are normally deposited and then plasma-etched with holes at aspect ratios of 40-80, the hardest and most fluorocarbon-hungry step in 3D NAND. Instead, define the hole lattice once at the bottom as metal seed dots and grow the stack around them. For each tier, selective CVD tungsten grows ~30 nm only on the exposed W pillar tops (selectivity holds for ~100 nm per cycle), a dielectric (SiO2 or SiN, alternating by tier) grows only on dielectric with a short-lived inhibitor on the W, and an in-situ NF3/H2 etch-back removes stray W nuclei. After the last tier the W pillars are dissolved, leaving vertical holes through the whole stack, aligned by construction.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #2 (3D needs one HAR etch through all tiers; bow, twist and CD variation), A2 (fluorocarbon/PFAS-adjacent etch gases and cryo-etch tool dependence).
ideas.step_change_claim: [SPECULATIVE] Eliminates the high-aspect-ratio mold etch: AR 38 (64 tiers) to 77 (128 tiers) with zero plasma etch and no bow or twist; hole CD set by the seed, not by depth.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: 64 x 60 nm = 3.84 um; 100 nm holes -> AR 38 (128 tiers: AR 77). Selective W window ~100 nm per cycle (Saraswat 1984, cited in US 4,741,928) vs 30 nm per tier: 3x margin. Defects: stray nuclei at 0.1 (0.01)/cm2 per layer x 128 layers = 12.8 (1.28) shorts/cm2 before etch-back, so each etch-back must remove >99.9% of nuclei. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-21)

ideas.claim_short: Grow-the-hole: dual area-selective deposition builds a 64-128-tier mold around pillars, no HAR etch

ideas.name: Sequential periphery-over-cell for Si DRAM: lithographic vias instead of hybrid bonds
ideas.one_liner: Finish a conventional Si 1T1C array, Smart-Cut a thin crystalline Si layer on top, build the sense amps in it at 400-500 C, and reach every 64-128-cell bitline with a 100-200 nm lithographic via: per-segment sensing at 1-beta pitch with one wafer, not two.
ideas.mechanism: Keep a conventional high-temperature Si 1T1C array (1-beta-class cell with a short capacitor), finish it including its capacitor, cap it with oxide, and transfer a ~50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top by Smart Cut. Build the sense amplifiers, sub-wordline drivers and decoders in that layer with CEA-Leti-style 400-500 C n&p CMOS. Connect each 64-128-cell bitline segment to its sense amp with a lithographically aligned via (~100-200 nm, overlay ~5-10 nm) instead of a hybrid-bond pad (>=300-400 nm pitch, ~50-100 nm overlay). This delivers A1 white space 1 (one sense amp per short bitline) at 1-beta pitch without the bond-pitch wall and without the second periphery wafer of bonded periphery-under-cell.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 (capacitor), #7 (periphery area), #10 (voltage floor), the bond-pitch gap of A1 white space 1, and the doubled wafer cost of bonded periphery-under-cell.
ideas.step_change_claim: Capacitor 1.3 um -> 226-376 nm (AR 62 -> 11-18) with no mux; one wafer instead of two (vs bonded PUC); array efficiency ~0.51 -> ~0.7 (1.37x density).
ideas.first_principles_estimate: A lithographic via instead of a bond pad saves ~2 fF: 64 cells Cbl 6 fF -> Cs 0.93 fF -> 226 nm pillar; 128 cells 10 fF -> 1.56 fF -> 376 nm. Sense-amp area budget (open bitline, two segments per SA): 0.137 um2 (64 cells) or 0.274 um2 (128 cells), tight because a ~10-transistor latch at a 28 nm-class rule is ~0.2-0.3 um2 [ESTIMATE], so start with 128-cell segments or a 2:1 mux. (models/B3_3dprocess_estimates.py section B3-22)

ideas.name: ECC-paid capacitor: let the code, not the capacitor, carry the last 4 sigma
ideas.one_liner: Design the array for a raw bit error rate of 1e-4 and protect it with a strong per-line code, so the storage capacitor can be half as tall.
ideas.mechanism: Today's ~50 mV sense budget exists so that every one of ~1.7e10 cells reads correctly at ~7 sigma of sense-amp (SA) offset and coupling noise, with only on-die SEC as backup. Re-centre the array on a raw BER target of 1e-4 per read. A t=8 BCH code (80 check bits per 512 data bits) in the memory controller or HBM/CXL logic base die absorbs the errors; optionally the SA fires two extra comparator thresholds to hand one soft-information bit per cell to a NAND-style soft decoder. With dV_min of 26 mV instead of 50 mV, the ZrO2/TiN pillar storage node can hold ~2.7 fF instead of 5.4 fF on the same 512-cell bitline: ~640 nm tall instead of 1,300 nm. An SA's offset is static, so codewords run along the row (each bit through a different SA), and outlier SAs are fused out at test like today's column repair. The same rule gives a 0.6 fF cell on a 64-cell local bitline in a 3D tier.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 storage-capacitor charge wall (also #2 3D-tier capacitor and #4 HAR-etch capital); secondary #10 voltage floor
ideas.step_change_claim: Capacitor height 2.0x lower (1,300 -> ~640 nm, aspect ratio 62 -> 30) at a 1e-4 raw BER, or 2.5x lower (-> ~525 nm, AR 25) at 1e-3, for +9 to +21 points of check bits (15.6-27.3% vs DDR5's 6.25%). 3D or local-bitline tiers need only 0.5-0.6 fF instead of 1.2 fF.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: sigma_eff = 50 mV / 7.03 = 7.1 mV (A1's budget read as 1e-12 per bit). dV_min = sigma x z(BER): 33.8 mV at 1e-6, 26.4 mV at 1e-4, 22.0 mV at 1e-3. Cs_min = Cbl x dV / (V_sig - dV), with Cbl = 34.7 fF (512 cells) and V_sig = 0.37 V after 15% droop: 5.47 -> 3.52 -> 2.69 -> 2.21 fF. Pillar height scales with Cs: 1,300 -> 836 -> 640 -> 525 nm. Retention check: at Cs x0.49 the modelled 85 C tail BER at 64 ms is 3.1e-8, well inside the budget. BCH over 512 data bits, Poisson error count, <=1e-15 failure per codeword: t=8 (80 b, 15.6%) at 1e-4; t=14 (140 b, 27.3%) at 1e-3. A 1 KB page-level code needs only 2.7% at 1e-4, but it forces page-granular decode. Fast path: P(any error in 592 b at 1e-4) = 5.7%, so ~94% of reads need only a syndrome check. (models/B4_architecture_estimates.py card01)

evidence.title: EDEN (MICRO 2019)
evidence.shows: Commodity DRAM run outside its voltage/latency margins produces a measurable, tolerable BER: the margin is real and tradeable (via search snippet)

ideas.novelty: TWIST on known. NAND has run LDPC with soft sensing for a decade, and ArchShield (Georgia Tech, ISCA 2013) tolerates 1e-4 fault rates, but both treat errors as defects to survive. Deliberately spending the ECC margin to shrink the DRAM capacitor (designing the array to a raw-BER target) does not appear in the public DRAM literature I found [UNVERIFIED absence].
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) Random-access latency: a t=8 BCH decode adds ~3-10 ns on errored reads, and partial writes become read-modify-write. (2) Errors are not iid: variable-retention-time (VRT) cells, pattern-dependent bitline coupling and temperature drift of SA offset cause bursts a 512-bit t=8 code can miss. (3) Half the charge (~8,800 signal electrons instead of ~17,700) means softer targets for alpha/neutron upsets and row hammer.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Check the syndrome on every read (an XOR tree, under 1 ns) and run the full decode only when it is nonzero, so ~94% of reads take the fast path. Keep writes at full-line granularity, which matches 64 B GPU and CPU lines. (2) Interleave codewords across mats and bitline pairs, measure pattern sensitivity on a test chip, and add a page-level outer code (2.7%) as a second layer. (3) Pair the cell with oxide-channel access devices, which have no Si junction (lower SER cross-section), and with B4-10 Row-RAID for hammer tolerance.
ideas.million_dollar_demo: Two parts, ~$0.6M total. (a) ~$60k: measure the real BER-vs-margin curve and its burst statistics on 50-100 commodity DDR4/DDR5 chips with an FPGA DRAM tester, using reduced tRCD and voltage as proxies for reduced signal (EDEN-style). (b) ~$350-500k: a 28/22 nm MPW test chip with a 256 kb 1T1C MIM (or gain-cell) array. Storage capacitance is selectable at 1x, 0.5x and 0.35x at a fixed Cs/Cbl ratio scale. On-chip are an 80-bit BCH decoder and soft-threshold sense amps. Measure post-ECC failure rate vs capacitor size at 25-105 C.
ideas.resource_angle: Halves HAR etch depth and capacitor wall area per wafer, so fewer fluorocarbon HAR-etch minutes and ~half the ZrO2/TiN ALD precursor. It opens Ru-free, Hf-lean short stubs that obey A2's element rule, and lowers capital per bit (HAR etch and ALD are among the most tool-intensive DRAM steps). No change to EUV use.
ideas.us_buildable: Test chip on a GlobalFoundries 22FDX (Malta, NY) or TSMC 28 nm MPW via university programmes; FPGA characterisation in any university lab; capacitor-split arrays at Albany NanoTech (NY CREATES) or Purdue Birck.
ideas.lens: ARCHITECTURE: DO DRAM'S JOB WITH LESS DRAM
ideas.triage_reason: Gaussian-offset statistics and BCH arithmetic are correct. The physics risks are non-iid errors (VRT, pattern coupling) and soft errors on ~8,800-electron cells; all measurable on FPGA rigs.
ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: measured error bursts at a 26 mV margin exceed t=8 per 512 b at >1e-15 per codeword.
ideas.claim_short: Design the array for raw BER 1e-4 + BCH t=8: capacitor 2x shorter (1,300 -> 640 nm)

ideas.name: Scrub-as-refresh: 1-second refresh, page-level code, lazy scrub
ideas.one_liner: Refresh every 1 s instead of every 64 ms, and let a 2% page-level code plus a 60 s scrub clean up the ~1e-5 cells that leak out in between.
ideas.mechanism: Each 1 KB DRAM page gets ~2% spare columns holding a BCH code (t=12 over GF(2^14)). The refresh engine restores rows about every second with a plain activate-precharge; the array itself is unchanged. A background scrubber decodes and rewrites each row about once a minute, so errors from weak and VRT cells can accumulate for at most one scrub period. Decoding at every refresh would eat most of the savings, so the scrub is lazy. Three add-ons stretch the interval further. (a) Per-subarray canary rows with undersized caps set the interval from measured leakage at the actual temperature, not from the 85 C 6.4-sigma worst case. (b) Retention errors only go one way (charged -> discharged, polarity known per true/anti cell), so an asymmetric (Z-channel) code needs fewer parity bits. (c) A write encoder flips 64-bit words to minimise how many cells sit charged. Fast-path reads use the existing on-die SEC; the page code is consulted only when an error is detected.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 access-device leakage tail -> refresh energy, tRFC availability loss and multi-level infeasibility
ideas.step_change_claim: ~15x less refresh energy, scrub included. Refresh busy time drops from 7.6% to 0.5% at 16 Gb, or from 20.5% to 1.3% at 64 Gb. All on today's Si 1T1C cell, for ~2% parity.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Retention-tail model [ESTIMATE]: BER(t) = 3.6e-9 x (t / 64 ms)^3 at 85 C. It is calibrated to RAIDR-era '~1,000 cells per 32 GB below 256 ms' with a 4x temperature derate. At 1 s the BER is 1.4e-5; x3 for VRT accumulation gives 4.2e-5. A 1 KB page BCH at <=1e-15 per codeword needs t=12: 168 b = 2.05%. Energy: baseline 46 fJ per bit-refresh x 15.6/s = 719 fJ/s per bit. With refresh at 1 s plus a syndrome every 60 s (14x12/2 XORs per bit x 2 fJ = 168 fJ/bit), it is 49 fJ/s, x14.7 lower; decoding at every refresh would give only x3.4. A 64 GB RDIMM's refresh drops from 0.49 W to ~33 mW. tRFC/tREFI: 295/3,900 = 7.6% -> 0.48%; 1,600/7,800 = 20.5% -> 1.3%. Charge-minimising encoding (30% of cells charged instead of 50%) stretches the interval only x1.19, so it is a garnish. (card02)

RAIDR (CMU, ISCA 2012) bins rows by retention; Intel's Hi-ECC (ISCA 2010) used multi-bit ECC to stretch eDRAM refresh [UNVERIFIED, training knowledge]; ArchShield maps faults. New here are three things: an in-bank page-level code with lazy scrub (decode every ~60 refreshes, not every one), a canary-row closed loop, and asymmetric codes matched to one-directional retention errors.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) VRT cells hop between long and short retention, so the weak population is unstable and bursts can exceed t. (2) Data-pattern dependence (bitline and wordline coupling) shifts retention by several times and is hard to bound. (3) Fewer refreshes leave more time for disturb to build up between restores. CryoGuard saw hammer-like failures when refresh was cut.

(2) Write worst-case data patterns into the canary rows. (3) Decouple hammer protection from refresh cadence with targeted victim refresh or B4-10 Row-RAID.

ideas.name: Lifetime-leased refresh: streamed and dead data are never refreshed
ideas.one_liner: The host tells the memory how long each region lives and how often it is read; rows that are streamed every decode step, or already dead, never get a REF command.
ideas.mechanism: A lease table in the memory controller (or HBM base die) puts each 2 MB region in one of three classes. (i) 'Dead': freed pages, retired KV. (ii) 'Streamed with period <= P': weights and live KV in LLM decode, read every token. (iii) 'Normal'. Class (ii) rows are restored as a side effect of every full activation. A per-region activation timestamp certifies that each row was opened within tREF, and the controller issues a targeted refresh only for rows that miss the deadline. Class (i) rows get no refresh at all. For most of an inference HBM, the all-bank REF command and its tRFC blackout disappear. A further step is an HBM bin specified for 'access-guaranteed' use, with a relaxed retention screen. Dies that fail today's 32 ms retention test become usable for weights.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh (energy and tRFC bandwidth loss) and #5 (bandwidth); A2 #1 capital (more good dies per wafer from a relaxed retention screen)
ideas.step_change_claim: Refresh energy -> ~0 for streamed and dead regions, and 5-15% more usable HBM bandwidth in bandwidth-bound decode (x1.05-1.18 tokens/s), with no cell change. General servers with 30-50% dead memory get refresh energy x0.5-0.7.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Full-HBM sweep time = capacity / bandwidth: 141 GB / 4.8 TB/s = 29 ms; 192 GB / 8 TB/s = 24 ms; 288 GB / 16 TB/s = 18 ms. All are under the 32 ms hot tREF, so decode-resident data is implicitly refreshed. Refresh power is small: 36 GB stack = 2.9e11 b x 46 fJ / 32 ms = 0.41 W (3.3 W per 8 stacks). The prize is time: recovering a 5/10/15% refresh blackout gives x1.053/1.111/1.176 throughput when decode is bandwidth-bound. (card03)

ideas.novelty: TWIST on known. Smart Refresh (MICRO 2007) skips recently accessed rows and ESKIMO (MICRO 2009) skips freed memory [both UNVERIFIED, training knowledge]. RANA (Tsinghua 2018) and Kelle (NYU 2025) do lifetime-aware refresh in on-chip eDRAM. ideas.show_stoppers: (1) An activation restores the cell fully only if tRAS is honoured; controllers that close rows early (restore truncation) void the guarantee. (2) Access patterns change (batch shrink, pre-emption, stalls), leaving rows unread past the deadline. (3) Streaming toggles every wordline every step; neighbours see two disturb events per sweep.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Specify a 'full-restore' activation mode. (2) Use a deadline-driven fallback refresh from a timestamp table (~KB per GB); the controller reacts within one tREF. (3) Each neighbour is itself restored every sweep, so the disturb count per restore stays at ~2, orders of magnitude below any HCfirst.

ideas.name: Significance-split memory: gold-grade sign/exponent, sand-grade mantissa
ideas.one_liner: Split every BF16/FP8 tensor into protected, entropy-coded sign+exponent rows and unprotected, slowly refreshed, low-voltage mantissa rows: 1.58x more values per DRAM bit and 3.7x less refresh.
ideas.mechanism: The memory controller (GPU or HBM base die) splits tagged tensors (weights, KV, activations) into bit-plane groups placed in different banks, so both are fetched in parallel. Sign and exponent are Huffman-coded to ~3 b (entropy ~2.6 b of 8) and stored in normal rows with ECC and standard refresh. The 7 mantissa planes go to 'approximate' banks with four relaxations: no ECC parity, refresh at ~1 s (raw BER ~1e-5), an optional separate lower VARY rail (~0.75 V), and lower-swing I/O lanes run at BER ~1e-6. Dies or subarrays that fail exact screening (weak cells, high-offset SAs) are binned for mantissa duty instead of scrapped. Ordinary data stays exact; a page-attribute bit selects the mode.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh, #10 array voltage/energy, #5 interface energy; capacity per wafer (A2 #1)
ideas.step_change_claim: For BF16 tensors: x1.58 capacity per DRAM bit (18 -> 11.4 cells per value incl. ECC), x3.7 less refresh energy per value, ~x2 less array energy and ~x2.8 less I/O driver energy on mantissa planes. FP8 x1.41; FP4 x1.18: the lever shrinks as formats narrow.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: BF16 with 12.5% ECC = 16 x 1.125 = 18 cells. Split: (1 + 2.9 b Huffman exponent) x 1.125 = 4.4, plus 7 mantissa = 11.4 -> x1.58. Refresh per value: (4.4 + 7 x 64 ms/1 s)/18 = 0.27. Array CV^2 at 0.75 V: (0.75/1.05)^2 = 0.51. Link: Q falls from 7.94 (1e-15) to 4.75 (1e-6), so swing x0.60 and voltage-mode driver energy x0.36. FP8 E4M3: 9 -> 6.4 cells (x1.41). FP4 E2M1: 4.5 -> 3.8 (x1.18). Tolerances: mantissa BER 1e-5 (RangeGuard), KV mantissa 1e-4 (SHIELD); 1 s refresh gives 1.4e-5 at 85 C (B4-02 model). (card04)

(2) Bit-plane layout breaks the native word layout: one 64 B GPU sector now needs two activations in two banks (more activation energy, bank conflicts). (3) Separate VARY rails per bank cost die area and test complexity.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Calibrate tolerance per tensor, with a 'promote' bit that moves sensitive layers to exact banks. (2) Bank-parallel placement hides the latency; activation is ~0.18 pJ/b when streaming, small next to the savings. (3) Ship the refresh/ECC/I/O policies first, which need no die change; add voltage domains in a later die.

ideas.name: Approximate 4-level DRAM for low-order planes and 2-bit KV
ideas.one_liner: Two bits per ordinary 1T1C cell, without the 3x capacitor exact multi-level DRAM needed, by storing only data whose level errors are harmless.
ideas.mechanism: A 2-bit DAC-driven write driver writes one of four levels (0, 0.35, 0.70, 1.05 V). Reads use charge sharing followed by a 3-threshold successive sense, with extra reference levels from split reference bitlines as in the 1997 4-level 4 Gb DRAM. Gray coding makes an adjacent-level error a +/-1 LSB error of the 2-bit field. MLC rows hold only data classes that tolerate ~1e-3 level error: KIVI-style 2-bit KV (one element per cell), the low mantissa planes of BF16 (with B4-04), and MX/FP4 element codes whose shared scales stay protected. Exact data stay single-level. On short bitlines (128 cells, e.g., with sense amps under the array) the same scheme becomes exact.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #1 (bits per capacitor) and #4 litho-bound density/capital
ideas.step_change_claim: 2x bits per cell for approximate data on the existing 1-beta array: KV capacity x2 vs single-level 2-bit storage, and BF16 with the B4-04 split x2.28 vs ECC'd BF16. At 128-cell bitlines the same circuit reaches exact-grade error rates (6.5e-15).
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Cs 5.41 fF, Cbl 34.7 fF: charge-sharing attenuation 0.135. Single-level fresh signal = 0.525 V x 0.135 = 71 mV. Four levels: level gap at the cell 0.35 V; half-gap on the bitline 23.6 mV = 3.32 sigma (sigma 7.1 mV), so the level error is 9e-4 per read when fresh. At 128 cells (Cbl 11.7 fF) the half-gap is 55 mV = 7.8 sigma, a 6.5e-15 error. The 1997 4-level 4 Gb DRAM needed ~3x the capacitor for exactness (patent citation). Capacity: 2-bit KV goes from 2 cells to 1. BF16 split: 4.4 protected + 3.5 MLC cells = 7.9 vs 18 -> x2.28. Cost: the droop budget per level is a third of single-level, so ~3x more refresh per cell for equal error, or accept age-dependent error (B4-06). (card05)

ideas.novelty: TWIST on known. Exact 4-level DRAM was built (ISSCC 1997) and abandoned because it needed 3x the capacitance and slow sensing, and B1-05 revisits exact 2-bit 1T1C on oxide cells. (2) Combine with B4-02 scrubbing or B4-13 cool operation (droop 4-18x slower). (3) Restore from the column latch through a shared DAC every 8-16 bitlines; or move multi-level tiers to non-destructive oxide gain cells (A3 white space 1).

ideas.name: Graceful-forgetting KV memory: leakage as the eviction policy [SPECULATIVE]
ideas.one_liner: Store KV magnitudes as multi-level charge that sags with age, so old tokens fade toward zero with no refresh, while attention sinks and heavy hitters are leased for refresh.
ideas.mechanism: KV elements are stored sign-separated: the sign sits in exact rows, the magnitude as a 4- or 8-level charge in true-cell polarity, so leakage only ever reduces magnitude. Rows holding the recent window, attention-sink tokens and controller-flagged heavy hitters are refreshed under a lease (B4-03). All other KV rows are never refreshed. Over seconds to minutes their magnitudes droop level by level. A fully discharged row reads as all zeros, and the allocator reclaims it on zero-detect. The model sees a continuous 'forgetting curve' resembling H2O/StreamingLLM-style eviction, at zero refresh energy. Training or fine-tuning with the decay model (as RANA did for CNNs) teaches the network to expect it.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh; KV capacity pressure on HBM (#5/#6)
ideas.step_change_claim: [SPECULATIVE] KV refresh energy -> 0 outside the leased window, with automatic capacity reclamation. Long-context KV footprint is bounded by the forgetting time constant rather than by context length.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: KV per token for a 70B-class model (8 KV heads x 128 x 80 layers x K,V x 2 B) is 328 KB; 128k tokens is 43 GB. Refresh costs 2.6e6 b x 46 fJ / 64 ms = 1.9 uW per stored token, while recomputing that token's KV costs ~0.14 J (2 x 70e9 FLOP at ~1 pJ/FLOP). Refresh beats recompute for any lifetime under ~74,000 s, so forgetting must replace refresh outright rather than be repaired by recompute. Decay spread: cell-leakage sigma_ln = 0.6-1.0 gives a 4.7-13x spread between 10th- and 90th-percentile decay times, so forgetting is randomised element by element, not token by token. (card06)

(2) Temperature-tracking canary rows (B4-02) turn decay into a calibrated 'age'. (3) In non-destructive oxide gain cells (A3 white space 1), reads do not refresh.

The idea rests on attention tolerating lognormally distributed per-element dropout, which rotates K vectors: an unproven ML premise, not a physics violation.

ideas.name: Tensor-aware codec in the memory controller (hardware DFloat11 + optional lossy KV)
ideas.one_liner: Entropy-code BF16 exponents at HBM line rate in the GPU memory path, so every stack holds and delivers ~1.47x more weights, losslessly.
ideas.mechanism: A codec in each GPU memory partition, with a matching engine in the HBM4 logic base die for capacity management, Huffman-codes the 8-bit exponents of tagged BF16 tensors. About 40 symbols are used, ~2.6 b entropy. Sign and mantissa are packed raw, 32 values per 64 B sector -> ~44 B. Fixed-rate block coding (32 exponents in a 96-112 b budget with an escape code) keeps random access at sector granularity. An optional lossy mode, under software control, applies KIVI-style per-channel K / per-token V 2-bit quantisation with a full-precision residual window. Unlike LZ-class CXL compressors (Marvell Structera, ZeroPoint: 2-3x on general data), this codec targets floating-point tensors, which LZ compresses poorly.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 interface energy and #6 HBM capacity tax; A2 #1 capital per bit
ideas.step_change_claim: Lossless x1.47 effective capacity and bandwidth for BF16 weights and activations, saving ~17.8 pJ of interface energy per value for ~0.2-0.5 pJ of decode. The lossy KV mode gives up to 2.6x peak memory.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: BF16: 16 b -> 1 + 2.9 + 7 = 10.9 b, x1.47 (DFloat11 reports ~70% size, ~11 b). Energy saved: (16 - 10.9) b x 3.5 pJ/b = 17.8 pJ per value, vs ~0.2-0.5 pJ Huffman decode in 5 nm-class logic [ESTIMATE]. Throughput: 16 TB/s / 2 B = 8e12 values/s per GPU; at 4 symbols per cycle and 2 GHz that is ~1,000 decoders of ~0.005 mm^2, ~5-10 mm^2 [ESTIMATE]. Placement matters: decoding in the base die saves capacity and TSV/core energy only, while decoding in the GPU memory controller also saves the ~2.5 pJ/b interposer path (A1). (card07)

(2) Table-driven decoders at 4 symbols/cycle need ~5-10 mm^2, under 1% of a reticle-size GPU. (3) For MX/FP8 formats, apply the same idea to shared scales and element histograms (~1.1-1.3x).

Synthesise to an academic 7 nm PDK (ASAP7) for area/power (~$120k). Optionally tape out a decoder slice on a 22 nm MPW (~$150k).

ideas.name: Compression-funded ECC: compressible rows earn slow refresh for free
ideas.one_liner: Every 64 B line that compresses by >=10 B carries a t=7 BCH code in the freed space, so rows of compressible data can be refreshed every 0.5-1 s at zero capacity cost.
ideas.mechanism: On write, the controller compresses each line: exponent Huffman for float tensors, base-delta-immediate or zero-run for integers and pointers. If the result is <=54 B, it appends 70 parity bits (t=7 BCH over GF(2^10)) in the same 64 B slot and sets a mode bit in the existing ECC/metadata side-band. A per-row counter tracks whether every line in the row is in 'strong' mode; strong rows move to a slow refresh bin (RAIDR-style Bloom filter) and weak rows stay at 64 ms. A line that becomes incompressible demotes its row immediately, the safe direction. Reads run the full decode only when the cheap syndrome is nonzero.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #3 refresh
ideas.step_change_claim: 8-16x lower refresh energy (0.5-1 s interval) on fully compressible rows at zero capacity overhead. Float tensors compress to ~44 B per line, so this covers most of an AI accelerator's DRAM.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Line = 512 b. BCH t=7 needs 70 b (~9 B), so the payload must be <=54 B including a 1 B header. A BF16 line of 32 values x 10.9 b is ~44 B. Retention BER at 85 C (B4-02 model): 0.5 s -> 1.7e-6 and 1 s -> 1.4e-5, both inside the 1e-4 design point; 2 s -> 1.1e-4 is marginal. Refresh energy x0.128 (0.5 s) or x0.064 (1 s). (card08)

ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) The allocator places tensors in dedicated rows; AI data is homogeneous within a tensor. (2) Demotion is immediate and safe; promotion is lazy. (3) The syndrome fast path, as in B4-01.

ideas.claim_short: Compression-funded ECC: compressible rows refreshed every 0.5-1 s at zero capacity cost

ideas.name: Top-k KV from in-memory scoring of MSB-plane sketches
ideas.one_liner: Store the KV cache bit-plane-major so its top 4 planes are a free sketch; score the sketch inside the memory and fetch full-precision K/V only for the ~2% of tokens that matter.
ideas.mechanism: Keys are quantised per channel to INT8 (KIVI-style) and stored as bit planes. The 4 MSB planes live in a PIM-capable tier (HBM-PIM or LPDDR5X-PIM). The low planes and V live in a cheaper capacity tier (LPDDR or CXL DRAM). Each decode step broadcasts the query to bank-level units, which compute approximate q.k scores from the MSB planes with bit-serial adds at the sense-amp stripe or the existing PIM MAC units, and return only scores (2 B per token per KV head). The GPU picks the top-k tokens (k ~ 1-4k) and fetches their full K and V. Nothing is stored twice: the sketch is the high planes of the real data.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 data movement, #6 HBM capacity tax, #8 overfetch
ideas.step_change_claim: At 128k-token contexts: ~7x less KV traffic per decode step and ~8x less HBM capacity for KV, with full KV in a ~3x cheaper-per-bit tier. In-memory scoring cuts the sketch pass's interface traffic ~2,500x.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: 70B-class GQA KV = 328 KB/token, so dense attention reads 42.9 GB per step per sequence at 128k. Sparse: the sketch (4 of 16 planes of K) is 12.5% of KV, plus full K and V for the top 2,048 tokens (1.6%), = 6.04 GB per step -> x7.1. HBM holds 12.5% of KV -> x8. Scores: 2 B x 8 heads x 131,072 = 2.1 MB vs 5.37 GB of sketch -> x2,560. (card09)

Map scoring to commercially available UPMEM PIM DIMMs or an FPGA memory controller emulating PIM, and measure end-to-end tokens/s and energy (~$150-200k).

ideas.name: Row-RAID: in-bank XOR parity rows built by triple-row activation
ideas.one_liner: Keep an XOR parity row for every 32 rows, computed inside the subarray, so any one row of read-mostly AI data can be rebuilt after hammer flips or weak-cell failures.
ideas.mechanism: For read-mostly regions (weights, and KV after it is written), the controller issues in-DRAM bulk-bitwise sequences that accumulate one parity row per group of 32 rows in a subarray. These are Ambit-style triple-row activation for AND/OR plus a dual-contact-cell NOT, composed into XOR. Group membership is interleaved so physically adjacent rows (the +/-1 and +/-2 victims of any aggressor) fall in different groups. Per-line ECC (on-die SEC or B4-01's BCH) detects a damaged row. The controller then XORs the other 31 rows and the parity inside the subarray and writes the reconstruction back. A write to a protected row updates parity with two in-DRAM XORs (old ^ new).
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #9 row hammer and #3 weak cells; unlocks tighter pitch and smaller Cs (B4-01)
ideas.step_change_claim: Row-hammer and weak-row tolerance for read-mostly data at ~3% capacity, instead of PRAC's <13% performance overhead today and up to 94% for future chips. Any single row per group may lose all its bits.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Overhead is 1/32 = 3.1% (1/16 = 6.2%, 1/64 = 1.6%). Parity build: 31 XORs x ~6 row cycles x 50 ns = 9.3 us per group, once per weight load [ESTIMATE]. Ambit: ~1% die area, 32x performance and 35x energy on bulk bitwise ops. Hammer threshold trend: 4.8K at LPDDR4-1y, extrapolated ~0.5-1K by 2026 (A1). (card10)

ideas.name: Erasure-coded memory stacks: 16+2 dies, any two may fail
ideas.one_liner: Build 16-high stacks with 2 parity dies so two bad dies or bond layers are tolerated, turning hybrid-bonding yield collapse into a 12.5% die overhead.
ideas.mechanism: Treat the dies of an HBM-class (or 3D wafer-bonded) stack like disks in RAID-6. Data channels are striped across dies with rotating parity computed in the logic base die. When a die fails (at stack test or in the field), the base die reconstructs its channels from the others in degraded mode, or remaps them to a spare die (simpler, preferred at test). Signal paths crossing a failed bond are protected by redundant TSV/bond pads with per-layer bypass, or by contactless inductive-coupling links, so one die's failure does not sever the chain. Power gets per-layer isolation switches. This lets stacks use non-known-good dies and imperfect bonds.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM TSV/stacking tax (hybrid-bonding yield across 16-20 bonds); A2 #1 capital per good bit
ideas.step_change_claim: At 95% per-die-in-stack yield, 16-high stack yield rises from 44% to 94% with 16+2: 1.9x fewer dies per good stack-bit. At 90% yield the gain is 3.5x; at 98%, 1.2x.

evidence.shows: HBM hybrid bonding pushed to 16-high HBM4E at the earliest because of multi-bond yield (CROSS-REF A1)

ideas.novelty: TWIST on known. Chipkill/SDDC across DIMM chips and RAID across disks are decades old, and HBM already has TSV redundancy and in-channel ECC. Die-level erasure coding across a stack, to accept non-known-good dies and imperfect bonds, has no public implementation that I found.
ideas.show_stoppers: (1) The serial TSV/bond chain: a power-ground short or open at layer k can kill every die above it, which no erasure code can fix. (2) Bandwidth: HBM maps channels to dies, so parity updates cost write bandwidth and degraded mode costs read bandwidth. (3) Thermal and height limits for 18 dies in 775-1,000 um.
ideas.revival_or_workaround: (1) Per-layer power isolation, redundant power TSVs, and contactless signal coupling (ThruChip-style inductive links, Keio [UNVERIFIED performance]). (2) Spare-die remap for test-time failures, and erasure only for field failures. Inference data is read-mostly, so parity-update cost is small. (3) Thinner dies (~30-40 um) are already planned for 16-20-high.

Thinned daisy-chain test dies carry redundant TSVs and power switches, bonded at a university/national-lab hybrid-bonding facility. An FPGA base-die emulator does remap and parity; intentionally open one layer and show bypass and reconstruction.

ideas.revival_condition: Alive. Kill test: dominant stack failures are power/ground shorts that kill every die above the fault.

ideas.name: Weight-streaming DRAM die: few banks, wide rows, no refresh
ideas.one_liner: A DRAM die built only for LLM weights, which are read in the same order every token. It sheds most of HBM's 35-45% area tax by dropping random-access machinery and refresh.
ideas.mechanism: HBM4 dies carry 256 banks and wide internal datapaths to serve random access from many pseudo-channels. A weight stream instead reads the same addresses in the same order every decode step. A streaming die uses ~16 large banks whose full rows are latched into a row-wide output FIFO and shifted onto TSVs, and a programmable sequencer replaces command decoding and per-bank state machines. It has no REF logic or refresh timers, because use refreshes every row (B4-03), with only a minimal self-refresh for idle. Mats and bitlines can be longer wherever the stream hides latency. It keeps the HBM base-die and TSV interface, so it stacks or sits beside HBM4 and HBF.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM tax, #7 periphery overhead, #3 refresh
ideas.step_change_claim: ~1.3-1.5x less silicon per bit than HBM for the weight-holding share of accelerator memory (array efficiency ~0.36 -> 0.45-0.55), plus zero refresh. It lands between HBM (3x DDR5 wafer/bit) and HBF.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: DDR5 array efficiency is 0.508 (A1). An HBM die is ~40% larger, so ~0.36. A streaming die at 0.45/0.50/0.55 needs x0.81/0.73/0.66 of HBM's area per bit. With ~10% better stack yield (fewer circuits), wafer per bit falls from ~3x DDR5 to ~1.8-2.2x DDR5 [ESTIMATE]. (card12)

ideas.name: GRS-linked LPDDR 'HBM-lite' on an organic substrate
ideas.one_liner: Near-HBM bandwidth and pJ/bit from commodity LPDDR dies on an ordinary organic substrate, using ground-referenced single-ended links, without HBM's ~3x wafer-per-bit tax.
ideas.mechanism: Stacks of standard LPDDR5X/6 dies (wire-bonded or face-to-face pairs) sit on an organic package beside a small logic buffer die. The LPDDR dies talk to the buffer over ~1-2 mm unterminated traces. The buffer talks to the accelerator over ground-referenced signalling (GRS: single-ended, a charge-pump negative rail, forwarded clock) at 20-25 Gb/s per pin across 5-30 mm of organic substrate. There is no silicon interposer and no TSV in the DRAM. Ten to sixteen such packages around an accelerator give HBM-class aggregate bandwidth.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM tax and #5 interface energy (held near HBM); A2 capital and CoWoS interposer capacity
ideas.step_change_claim: ~3x fewer DRAM wafers per bit than HBM at 2.7-3.4 pJ/bit (HBM3E: 3.44), with no silicon interposer.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Energy = LPDDR core ~1.5 + short LPDDR I/O ~0.5 + GRS 0.54-1.17 + buffer 0.2 = 2.7-3.4 pJ/b [ESTIMATE; GRS figures REPORTED]. Wafer: LPDDR is ~1x DDR5 per bit, HBM ~3x (Micron). Shoreline: ~50 lanes/mm x 25 Gb/s = 156 GB/s per mm per routing layer, so a 4 TB/s target needs ~26 mm of shoreline on 1 layer or 13 mm on 2 [ESTIMATE]. (card15)

ideas.name: HBF weight tier with read-disturb-aware 'weight mode'
ideas.one_liner: Put inference weights in High-Bandwidth Flash, but run it in pseudo-SLC with disturb-scheduled relocation, because reading every weight every token is exactly what NAND hates.
ideas.mechanism: HBF stacks NAND dies on TSVs behind an HBM-like interface (OCP spec August 2026: 256 GB/die, 512 GB per 16-high stack, ~1.6 TB/s read). Weights are written once per deployment, while KV and activations stay in DRAM. Each decode step reads every weight page, so a page sees 1e5-3e6 reads per day. Read disturb (pass-voltage stress on the unselected wordlines of a block) then forces periodic reclaim, that is, a rewrite. The 'weight mode' has four parts: program weights in pSLC, or TLC with relaxed retention; interleave each tensor across many blocks so read counts stay even; track per-block read counters and relocate before the disturb limit; and keep a second replica on another die to alternate reads when the disturb budget is tight.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #6 HBM tax; A2 #1 capital (NAND layers are deposition-defined, with no EUV)
ideas.step_change_claim: HBF claims 8-16x HBM capacity at similar cost. In endurance-safe pSLC weight mode it still gives ~3-5x HBM capacity per $, against HBM's ~3x DDR5 wafer cost per bit.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Reads per page per day = (stack bandwidth / model size) x 86,400: 400 GB on 1.6 TB/s -> 3.5e5; 100 GB -> 1.4e6; 50 GB -> 2.8e6. A disturb limit of 1e5-1e6 reads per block [UNVERIFIED] means 126-10,092 reclaim P/E cycles per year. TLC (~3k P/E [UNVERIFIED]) survives only the large-model, low-rate case; pSLC (~30-100k P/E) covers all. pSLC holds a third of TLC's capacity, so ~3-5x HBM per $ remains, given the 8-16x TLC claim. (card16)

ideas.name: Procedural weights: seeds plus coefficients, regenerated in the memory path
ideas.one_liner: Store weights as pseudo-random seeds plus a few coefficients and regenerate them at line rate in the memory controller: ~4 low-precision MACs replace 16 bits of DRAM per weight.
ideas.mechanism: Each block of ~8 weights is approximated as a linear combination of 3-4 pseudo-random basis vectors. An LFSR generates them from a 16-bit seed, weighted by 4-bit coefficients (SeedLM-style). Only seeds and coefficients (~3-4 b/weight) are stored in DRAM. A generator array in the GPU memory partition (or the HBM base die) expands them to BF16/FP8 on the way to the tensor cores. The LFSR and MACs cost ~0.3 pJ per weight, against ~14-56 pJ to fetch 4-16 bits over HBM.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 data movement and #6 HBM capacity (fewer bits stored and moved)
ideas.step_change_claim: 4-5.3x fewer stored bits than BF16, but only 1.0-1.33x vs FP4. The step is real only if accuracy at ~3 b/weight beats plain FP4/INT3 quantisation.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: 3 b/weight: x5.3 vs BF16, x1.33 vs FP4. 4 b: x4.0 / x1.0. Regeneration: ~4 MAC x 0.08 pJ = 0.32 pJ, vs 16 b x 3.5 pJ/b = 56 pJ to fetch [ESTIMATE]. Compute is ~100x cheaper than memory per weight, so any reconstruction using fewer than ~50 ops per weight saves energy. (card17)

ideas.name: Nested-precision bit-plane memory + self-speculative decoding
ideas.one_liner: Lay weights out bit-plane-major so the memory can serve a 2-4-bit draft of the same model from its top planes: draft cheaply, verify with all planes, and get 1.1-1.8x more tokens per byte of bandwidth.
ideas.mechanism: INT8/FP8 weights are quantised in a nested (Matryoshka-style) way, so the top 2 or 4 bit planes are themselves a usable low-precision model. The memory controller stores the planes in separate address ranges and streams 'planes 0-1', 'planes 0-3' or all of them, in 512 B-2 KB chunks that match DRAM bursts and pages. Decode is self-speculative: draft k tokens with the top planes only (25-50% of the weight bytes), then verify all k in one batched pass with every plane. No second model is stored.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 data movement (bandwidth per token) and #8 overfetch
ideas.step_change_claim: 1.1-1.8x effective decode bandwidth (weight reads per accepted token 0.89-0.55), with zero extra capacity.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: Expected tokens per verify E = (1 - a^(k+1)) / (1 - a); reads per token = (k*f + 1) / E. f=0.5, k=4, a=0.8: E 3.36, reads 0.89 (x1.12). a=0.9: E 4.10, reads 0.73 (x1.37). f=0.25, k=6, a=0.85: E 4.53, reads 0.55 (x1.81). (card18)

ideas.name: BitNet-native charge-sharing popcount PIM in commodity 1T1C
ideas.one_liner: With ternary LLM weights, decode is signed popcounts, and a DRAM subarray can count by charge sharing: open 8 rows at once and read the bitline voltage as a 3-bit count.
ideas.mechanism: Ternary weights {-1, 0, +1} are stored as two bit-masks (positive and negative) in 1T1C rows, and activations are bit-sliced (INT8 into 8 binary planes). For each activation plane, the controller first RowClones the selected weight rows, ANDed with the activation mask (Ambit-style), into dedicated compute rows. It then activates 8 compute rows at once on the same bitlines. Charge sharing gives a bitline voltage proportional to the number of charged cells (0-8), which a 3-bit flash ADC shared by 8-16 bitlines in the SA stripe digitises. A small near-bank adder shifts and accumulates the partial sums. Weights never leave the bank.
ideas.which_bottleneck: A1 #5 data movement and #8 overfetch (every activated bit is used)
ideas.step_change_claim: 12-35x lower energy per decode GEMV than reading ternary weights over HBM (0.39 J vs 0.011-0.033 J per token for a 70B ternary model), plus ~8x internal bandwidth.
ideas.first_principles_estimate: 70e9 weights x 1.58 b = 1.1e11 b. Over HBM at 3.5 pJ/b that is 0.39 J/token. In-bank at 0.1-0.3 pJ/b (amortised activation plus ADC) it is 0.011-0.033 J, i.e., x12-35. Popcount accuracy: with Cs sigma 5%, sigma_sum = sqrt(n) x 5%. n=8 gives 0.14 LSB (count error 4e-4); n=16 gives 1.2e-2; n=32 gives 7.7e-2. So use 8-row groups. (card19)
